title: google/agentmesh — Agent Mesh
content:
Agent Mesh is a private network for AI agents. A node runs next to an agent and gives it three things: a way to publish tools and models to the network, a way to find and call what other nodes publish, and an identity every other node can verify. Nodes connect directly when they can and through relays when they cannot, so the network works across laptops, containers, clusters and phones behind NAT.
Note: We have updated the name to Agent Mesh to better align with the goals of the project in the ecosystem.
Two properties hold everywhere:
- Nothing is reachable by default. A node exposes no services until its configuration says so, and no node may call a service the mesh policy has not granted. Grants are evaluated on service names, never on addresses.
- Identity comes from your identity provider. A node enrolls with an OpenID Connect token or a one-time bootstrap token, and the control plane turns that into a short-lived, offline-verifiable credential bound to the node's own key.
curl -sL https://google.github.io/agentmesh/install.sh | bash  # agentmesh-node, mcp-client and friends
agentmesh-node join https://bananas.sam-mesh.dev               # one-time login
agentmesh-node run --daemonize                                 # local MCP server on 127.0.0.1:8080
agentmesh-node skill install                                   # teach your agent to use it
Your agent now has tools that discover and call services across the mesh,
and an OpenAI-compatible endpoint that routes model requests to whoever
serves the model. bananas.sam-mesh.dev is a shared developer testnet with
no uptime promise; the quick start
walks through it, and your own mesh
runs a control plane on your laptop in one command.
To run a control plane of your own without installing anything, open a
GitHub codespace with the released binaries and run make testnet. It
starts on a public https URL that your laptop and phone can enroll into,
on your GitHub account's free quota:
The Codespaces guide has the steps, what persists and what stops.
google.github.io/agentmesh/docs is built from site/.
- Getting started: one node on the testnet, then a mesh of your own.
- Concepts: architecture, identity and enrollment, authorization, networking.
- Guides: exposing services, connecting agent clients, headless enrollment, Kubernetes, Cloud Run.
- Reference: every flag, configuration key, HTTP route and policy field.
- Preview: sandboxed agents and the mobile app, which work but are still settling.
- Contributing: building, testing and the local kind environment.
The repository has a dev container with the Go, Node and Python toolchains and Docker, so you can build and test in a codespace or in VS Code without installing anything:
Agent Mesh is pre-1.0. The node, routers, control plane, identity and policy model are stable in shape and exercised by the test suite and two public testnets; see ROADMAP.md for the release plan. Sandboxed agent blueprints and the mobile app are in preview.
Apache-2.0; see LICENSE. This is not an officially supported Google product, and it is not eligible for the Google Open Source Software Vulnerability Rewards Program.

report.summary: Google open-sources Agent Mesh, a private, identity-verified network that lets AI agents publish, discover, and call each other's tools and models across NATs and clouds.
report.background: The agent ecosystem has standardized rapidly on Anthropic's Model Context Protocol (MCP) for tool access and Google's Agent2Agent (A2A) for agent-to-agent coordination. But a gap remains: there is no default way for agents to securely find and call each other across laptops, containers, clusters, phones, and corporate networks behind NAT. Most teams hand-roll VPNs, tunnels, or API keys, which do not scale or enforce policy. Agent Mesh (renamed from an earlier project name to better fit the ecosystem) attacks this as infrastructure: a mesh layer that combines MCP tool serving, peer discovery, OIDC-based identity, service-name-based authorization, and relay fallback. It is Apache-2.0, pre-1.0, and explicitly not an officially supported Google product.
key_points: Agent Mesh runs a node beside each agent. That node publishes the agent's tools and models to the network, discovers and calls services published by other nodes, and holds an identity every peer can independently verify. Nodes connect peer-to-peer when possible and fall back to relays, so the same mesh spans laptops, containers, clusters, and phones behind NAT.

Security is deny-by-default. A node exposes nothing until configuration enables it, and no node can call a service unless mesh policy grants it. Grants are evaluated on service names, never on IP addresses, so services can move without rewriting rules. Identity comes from your existing identity provider via OpenID Connect or a one-time bootstrap token.

Enrollment is short-lived and offline-verifiable. The control plane converts an OIDC or bootstrap token into a credential bound to the node's own key, which other nodes can verify without calling home. This lets a fleet of agents authenticate each other without long-lived shared secrets or central per-request authorization.

Developer onboarding is a few commands: install via curl, join a mesh, run the daemon to start a local MCP server on 127.0.0.1:8080, and install a skill so the agent learns to use the mesh. Agents also get an OpenAI-compatible endpoint that routes model requests to whichever node serves the requested model.

Maturity is early but structured: the node, routers, control plane, identity, and policy model are stable in shape and exercised by tests and two public testnets. Sandboxed agent blueprints and a mobile app are in preview. It is Apache-2.0, not officially supported by Google, and ineligible for Google's OSS vulnerability rewards program.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Agent Mesh adds a missing infrastructure layer beneath MCP and A2A: identity, policy, discovery, and NAT traversal. If adopted, cross-company agent calls could look less like bespoke API integrations and more like joining a mesh. For developers, it offers a fast path to expose and reuse tools and models, plus a local OpenAI-compatible gateway, but it also introduces new concepts: enrollment, credentials, and service-name-based policy. For regular users, the payoff is agents that can borrow capabilities instead of every vendor rebuilding integrations, but the trade-off is early-stage tooling, a shared testnet with no uptime promise, and a new trust surface that must be governed carefully.
report.tools: To follow up, watch the google/agentmesh repository and ROADMAP.md, plus the docs on architecture, identity, authorization, and networking. Related projects: Model Context Protocol (MCP) for tool serving, Agent2Agent (A2A) for agent coordination, SPIFFE/SPIRE for workload identity, OIDC providers such as Okta, Auth0, or Google Identity, and tunnels like Cloudflare Tunnel or ngrok for NAT scenarios. Try the Codespaces guide and make testnet to run a control plane on GitHub's free quota.
